attributes.residual: SCHEDULE, single named mechanism, and OUR schedule is strictly BETTER than the target's. Target preheader: `li r0,8 / lis r3,HA / mtctr r0 / li r5,0 / addi r4,r3,LO / add r3,r4,r5`. Ours: identical but with `addi r4,r3,LO` and `li r5,0` transposed. The target therefore issues `addi r4` back-to-back with the `add r3,r4,r5` that consumes it, while ours separates them by a slot -- so this is NOT a latency-hiding choice the scheduler would prefer, it is a preheader emission-order tie-break between two independent initialisations (the loop-invariant base address and the induction offset). DECISIVE FREE EVIDENCE, recorded so nobody re-derives it: the same `case 7:` loop appears a third time in this TU, in CritterAllocType, which is FULLY MATCHED and whose target emits the BASE-FIRST order that ours emits here. In CritterAllocType the index is allocated to r3, the very register the `lis` result occupies, so base-first is FORCED there by a data dependency; in CritterLoadDone the index gets a fresh r5 and no dependency orders the pair. Two textually identical loops in one TU thus receive different preheader orders for register-allocation reasons -- the same proof shape as claim.law.zero-remat-choice-differs-between-identical-sibling-loops. UNPARK CONDITION: an allocator-level lever or a WebFrank permutation rule; no source spelling reached it. CritterLoadStartNext carries a byte-identical residual and the same verdict.
